name: The Authorship Rule
title: The Authorship Rule
answer: The Authorship Rule is a school-wide agreement that students must create their own work and disclose any AI help they use. It matters because it gives everyone a clear line, so a student cannot submit AI-generated art as their own and claim they did not know better. It also opens a real conversation about what makes creative work belong to a person.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: The rule exists because schools often lack any shared standard for AI in creative subjects, leaving students to guess and teachers to judge case by case. A student might turn in an image made in seconds and honestly think nothing was wrong. The simplest form of the rule is that the student makes the work and any AI assistance is disclosed. It does not ban AI outright. Instead it separates acceptable help, such as brainstorming or finding references, from presenting AI output as the student's own creation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice the rule allows AI in narrow, named ways. A student might use it to brainstorm ideas for a painting, locate reference images, or learn about an artist's techniques, and tools such as Canva for Education or Adobe Express for Education may be used to lay out a poster as long as the artwork and design choices remain the student's. What is not allowed is presenting work made by AI as their own. The AI use levels from Chapter 3 fit here, with most creative assignments marked at the lower levels. A few assignments may explore AI directly, such as comparing a student's drawing with a generated one and discussing the differences, and those should be clearly labeled. Figure 10.3 presents the rule in a form teachers can post and share with families.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no research evidence for the rule itself, so it rests on practice rather than study. It does cite one external point, drawn from UNESCO's guidance, which notes that the United States Copyright Office has said output generated by AI is not protected by copyright, because copyright protects only work that comes from human creativity (Miao & Holmes, 2023). The book presents this as a teaching point for older students rather than as proof that the rule works.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the rule itself: AI may support thinking and preparation, but the artwork and design choices must be the student's, and any help must be disclosed. Assignments that explore AI directly must be clearly labeled so they are not confused with ordinary creative work. The legal point about copyright is offered as a discussion topic for older students, not as legal advice. The decisions about where the line sits for a given assignment stay with the teacher and the school, who set the levels and label the exceptions.
